name: snail bead

attributes.attribute: formed naturally by a mass of snails
made water into a healing drink
kept bad luck away from the one who wore it

sources: Campbell, John Grigorson. Witchcraft and Second Sight in the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. Detroit: Signing Tree Press, 1970, 88.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The snail bead is a charm of old Scotland. It resembles the serpent stone. The bead was said to form in the wild, without work from a hand. It came from a mass of snails that gave out a strange fluid. The beads were few and hard to get. They carried a healing power. Set into a glass of water, the bead made the water into a healing drink. Worn on the body, it turned away bad luck. The Scottish folk carried the charm on their skin. Beads of this kind were valued because they were rare, and the one who owned one kept its power close. The record of the bead comes from Campbell and it holds a place among the Scottish talismans. As an object, the bead links the natural world and the belief of the people.
